item.title: Morgan Stanley IM says bond yields are rising for the right reasons, favours US and Japan
item.description:
Morgan Stanley IM’s view offers a more benign reading of the yield rise than fears of fiscal strain or a growth scare, and if markets adopt it, US equities could keep absorbing higher yields as long as earnings deliver. The house’s underweight in duration and preference for credit suggest it expects long-dated Treasuries to stay under pressure rather than rally. Its tilt toward Japan aligns with strong nominal growth there, while the underweight on Europe points to relative weakness in European stocks. For oil, the inflation component of high nominal growth is worth watching, since energy costs tied to the Iran war feed directly into it. The main risk to the thesis is a disappointing Q3 earnings season, which would remove the cushion Caron says is supporting equity prices.

---

Earlier:

  • Goldman Sachs says rising global bond yields reflect a growing competition for capital

---

Morgan Stanley’s investment arm reads the rise in Treasury yields as a sign that the US economy is running hot, and it is betting US earnings can stay one step ahead of borrowing costs.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley Investment Management, which oversees around $2 trillion, favours US and Japanese equities and is underweight Europe.
  • Jim Caron, CIO of its Portfolio Solutions Group, says higher yields reflect resilient nominal growth rather than economic stress, with US real growth plus inflation running at about 6.5%.
  • The US 10-year yield peaked at around 5.3% on 5 October this year before easing to around 5.1%.
  • The firm is underweight duration and overweight credit, and has cut interest rate sensitivity across its portfolios.
  • Caron said potential Democratic gains in November’s midterms could narrow US opportunities toward large, established companies such as AI hyperscalers.
  • He said private credit has moved past its correction phase, with more exits allowing capital to be deployed at today’s higher rates.

Morgan Stanley Investment Management says the rise in government bond yields this year reflects strong economic growth rather than stress, and is not yet a warning sign for equities, as it maintains a preference for US and Japanese stocks over those in Europe.

Jim Caron, chief investment officer of the Portfolio Solutions Group at the firm, which managed around $2 trillion in assets at the end of September, told journalists in a recent webinar that higher yields increasingly reflect resilient nominal growth. Nominal growth combines real economic expansion with inflation, and Caron put that figure at about 6.5% in the US. He pointed to firm growth, robust labour markets and productivity gains as factors supporting activity while helping to ease inflation pressure.

The US 10-year Treasury yield climbed to around 5.3% on 5 October, its high for the year, before easing to around 5.1%. Caron said such a move was natural given the pace of nominal growth, arguing that bonds are not signalling a slowdown and that yields are rising for sound reasons. In his view, bonds have taken a knock but are not broken.

The question for investors is when higher yields begin to weigh seriously on stocks. Caron’s answer rests on earnings. He said strong nominal growth points to healthy corporate cash generation and described expectations for third-quarter earnings as very robust. He argued that the US equity market is better placed than any other to benefit from that growth, and said Japan is also well positioned after a period of strong nominal growth.

That view offers a different explanation for the same trend highlighted by Goldman Sachs (link to post above), which has attributed the global rise in yields to intensifying competition for capital from government borrowing and AI investment. Both see higher yields as the new backdrop; they differ on whether it is driven mainly by demand for funding or by the strength of the economy itself.

In bonds, Morgan Stanley IM is underweight duration, overweight credit and has reduced interest rate sensitivity across its portfolios. On politics, Caron said potential Democratic gains in November’s midterm elections, and any pushback against the administration’s deregulation agenda, could narrow US opportunities and favour large, established firms such as AI hyperscalers.

On private markets, Caron said private credit has completed its correction phase after stress earlier this year in areas such as software. A pick-up in exits is creating room to deploy capital at today’s higher rates, he said, though he expects the next phase to be slower.

The third-quarter earnings season will be a key test of whether profits can continue to outpace the rise in borrowing costs.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs says rising global bond yields reflect a growing competition for capital
item.description:
If Goldman is right that higher yields reflect structural demand for capital rather than a temporary inflation scare, the pressure on long-dated bonds may prove persistent, keeping term premiums elevated across developed markets. For equities, the read-through is that index-level strength is resting heavily on earnings, so any disappointment from AI-linked leaders could expose valuations that have already compressed. Rising Japanese yields matter beyond Japan, since higher returns at home can draw domestic investors back from overseas markets and support the yen. Australian and UK bonds, already above 5%, stand out as the high-yield end of the developed world, which may support the Australian dollar and sterling on carry grounds. Higher government borrowing tied to energy security also links the bond story to oil, as elevated energy costs feed both fiscal needs and inflation risk.

---

Earlier:

  • Nasdaq and S&P rebounds; Dow slips

---

Governments and AI builders are both lining up for funding, and Goldman Sachs argues that higher yields are simply the price investors are now charging to stand in that queue.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs says higher government bond yields have become the global norm, with 10-year yields up in every major developed market this year.
  • Since January, 10-year yields have risen by around 100 bps in Japan, about 85 bps in the US and close to 80 bps in both the euro area and the UK.
  • UK and Australian 10-year yields are above 5%, while Japan’s is near 3% after years below zero.
  • The bank attributes the rise to intensifying competition for capital, as governments borrow for defence, energy security and infrastructure and companies raise record sums for AI infrastructure and data centres.
  • Goldman says choosing well now matters as much as market exposure, with bonds once again a real source of return but not always a reliable hedge for stocks.
  • The bank says S&P 500 forward valuations have slipped toward April’s lows even as the index sits near record highs, with strong earnings, especially in AI-linked names, masking the pressure.

Goldman Sachs says higher bond yields have become the global norm, arguing that a growing competition for capital, rather than a passing shock, explains why borrowing costs have climbed across every major developed market this year.

In a note, the bank highlighted the breadth of the move. Since January, the 10-year government bond yield has risen by around 100 basis points in Japan, about 85 basis points in the US and close to 80 basis points in both the euro area and the UK. Goldman said five of the six markets it tracks recorded their highest monthly average yield since at least 2019 in September. UK and Australian 10-year yields are now above 5%, while Japan’s is approaching 3%, a striking shift for a market where yields sat below zero for years.

The bank’s explanation centres on demand for funding. Many governments are borrowing more to pay for defence, energy security and infrastructure, while companies are raising record amounts to build AI infrastructure and data centres. Goldman said these combined needs are pushing up demand for capital, and investors are asking for greater compensation to lend. In the bank’s framing, higher yields are what that competition looks like in practice.

That environment, Goldman argues, rewards discrimination over broad exposure. The bank describes selectivity as the new source of excess return, saying that choosing well now matters as much as simply being invested. Higher starting yields have restored bonds as a genuine source of return, Goldman said, although they may not always offer a dependable hedge when stocks fall. Among equities, the bank sees companies that can fund their own growth, or that earn more than their cost of capital, as potentially better positioned.

Goldman also pointed to what it sees as rational behaviour in equity valuations. The forward multiple on the S&P 500 has drifted back toward the lows seen in April, even as the index trades near record highs. In the bank’s view, strong earnings growth, particularly among AI-linked companies, may be masking the valuation pressure that higher yields would otherwise put on share prices.

The implication is that equity strength is increasingly dependent on earnings delivery. If yields stay elevated and profit growth slows, the cushion that has protected headline index levels could thin, leaving investors more exposed to the gap between rising financing costs and corporate returns. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq and S&P rebounds; Dow slips
item.description:
U.S. stocks closed mixed to start the new trading week, with the Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 gaining more than 1% while the Dow industrial average edged lower.

After last week’s selling, buyers returned to some of the technology names. Amazon led the large-cap rebound with a gain of nearly 5%, while storage, semiconductor and software shares featured prominently among the strongest performers.

However, the gains were far from universal. More stocks declined than advanced on both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq. Buyers are making a play, but broader participation would give the recovery more credibility.

The closing numbers

  • Dow Industrial Average: fell 35.81 points, or 0.07%, to 51,966.60.

  • S&P 500: rose 33.20 points, or 0.43%, to 7,692.64.

  • Nasdaq Composite: rose 290.85 points, or 1.11%, to 26,430.89.

  • Russell 2000: rose 6.92 points, or 0.25%, to 2,728.29.

  • Nasdaq 100: rose 341.80 points, or 1.17%, to 29,529.35.

Amazon leads, with help from chips and software

Amazon was the standout among the major technology names, rising 4.98% to $262.45. Nvidia added 1.38% to $217.09, while Microsoft gained 0.84% to $533.52.

Apple did not join the advance, slipping 0.15% to $342.94. That divergence is another reminder that even within the largest technology companies, traders are picking their spots.

Some of the stronger individual performers included:

  • Western Digital: +6.12%.

  • SanDisk: +5.50%.

  • Datadog: +5.35%.

  • SK Hynix ADR: +4.67%.

  • Palantir: +4.36%.

  • Marvell: +4.06%.

The buying extended beyond technology. Celsius gained 5.43%, while Moderna rose 4.07%.

Dow weakness reflects a divided market

The Dow finished modestly lower, with 19 components declining and 11 advancing.

Amazon’s strong gain, together with advances in IBM (+1.85%), Nvidia (+1.38%) and UnitedHealth (+1.36%), helped cushion the downside. However, several financial, healthcare and other Dow components moved lower:

  • JPMorgan: −1.79%.

  • Amgen: −1.75%.

  • 3M: −1.66%.

  • Merck: −1.58%.

  • Verizon: −1.44%.

The result was a session where the technology-heavy indices delivered solid gains, but the average stock had a more difficult day.

Market breadth leaves buyers with work to do

The underlying participation figures were less encouraging than the headline index gains:

  • S&P 500: 166 stocks advanced versus 318 that declined.

  • Nasdaq: 1,432 advanced versus 1,768 that declined.

  • Nasdaq 100: 60 advanced versus 40 that declined.

  • NYSE: 611 advanced versus 1,181 that declined.

The Nasdaq 100 had better participation within its own group. Across the broader market, however, decliners held the advantage.

That does not erase the gains. It does tell traders that Monday’s rebound was concentrated. The next step for buyers is to hold those gains and bring more stocks along.

The trading lesson: look beneath the index

An index can rise even when more of its stocks fall. In a market-cap-weighted index such as the S&P 500, larger companies carry more influence. Strong gains in a handful of heavyweights can outweigh smaller declines across many other stocks.

For traders, the index provides the broader backdrop, but each stock still needs its own technical roadmap. A rising Nasdaq can help sentiment. Your stock still needs to get above—and stay above—its resistance levels.

Monday gave buyers some breathing room. Whether they can build on it is the next test.

item.title: NZDUSD buyers build momentum as the recovery approaches its next resistance test
item.description:
Buyers start to turn the technical picture around

The NZDUSD buyers have started to turn the shorter-term technical picture around after the prolonged move lower. The recovery has come in steps, with each break giving buyers a little more confidence. However, there is still work to do before the recent gains can develop into a more meaningful correction of the broader decline.

Thursday’s moving average break provided the catalyst

The first step came on Thursday when the price moved away from the 100- and 200-hour moving averages (blue and green lines on the chart above). Those moving averages help define the shorter-term bias and give traders a reference for risk. When the price can move above both and build distance from them, it suggests sellers are losing some control and buyers are becoming more willing to step in.

That move provided the catalyst. Friday’s break above the swing area between 0.56225 and 0.5633 provided the next piece of technical evidence (see lower yellow area on the chart above). 

Friday’s breakout gave buyers more confidence

Why does that matter? Swing areas identify levels where buyers and sellers have previously made decisions. When the price moves above a former ceiling, it forces traders to reassess. Sellers leaning against that resistance lose some of their technical protection, while buyers gain a level they can use to define risk on a pullback.

The break above 0.56225–0.5633 therefore strengthened the bullish shift and opened the door for the recovery to extend toward the next resistance zone between 0.5673 and 0.5686.

The next hurdle: 0.5673–0.5686

Several swing levels formed in that region during September before sellers pushed the price lower. As the price returns, traders will be watching to see whether sellers defend the area again or whether buyers can generate enough momentum to push through it.

For buyers, getting above the zone is one step. Staying above it is what would give the break more credibility. A brief move above resistance followed by a quick reversal would leave the market vulnerable to another rotation lower. Buyers would have had their shot, and a failure to hold the break would suggest sellers are still prepared to defend the broader downtrend.

A break higher targets the 38.2% retracement

A sustained move above 0.5686 would clear another obstacle and put the 38.2% retracement of the decline from the August high at 0.57258 in play.

That retracement is an important benchmark for judging the strength of the recovery. Buyers can make progress on the hourly chart while the broader move remains corrective. Reaching and eventually breaking the 38.2% level would add evidence that they are taking back more control. Until then, the recovery still has something to prove.

Former resistance becomes the support to watch

On the downside, the 0.56225–0.5633 swing area becomes the support zone to watch. The former ceiling now gives buyers an opportunity to show they can defend the breakout.

Holding above that area on a pullback would keep the recovery structure intact and give buyers a foundation for another push higher. A move back below it would weaken the breakout story and bring the hourly moving averages back into focus.

Follow the technical steps and define the risk

That is the value of following the technical steps. Each break creates a new target, but it also creates a reference for risk. Traders can judge the recovery by whether the price continues to clear resistance and then holds those levels as support.

The buyers have made progress. They moved away from the hourly moving averages and cleared the first swing area. Getting through 0.5673–0.5686—and staying above it—is the next test of their strength.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: China LPR preview: rates seen on hold for a 17th month after Q3 GDP beat
item.description:
A hold is widely expected and should be largely priced, so any reaction is likely to come only from a surprise. An unexpected cut (not gonna happen ... thats how unespected it'd be!) would probably weigh on the yuan, given the already wide gap between US and Chinese yields, while giving Chinese equities and property names a lift. The Australian and New Zealand dollars, often traded as proxies for Chinese growth, could firm on a cut as a sign of extra support for demand. For oil, any easing from the world’s largest crude importer would be a modest positive for demand, at a time when Iran war disruptions are already keeping supply risk elevated. A hold keeps the focus on liquidity tools such as a reserve requirement ratio cut as the more likely form of any future easing.

---

With growth back inside Beijing’s target range and the Fed tightening, the PBOC has little reason to move its lending benchmarks and good reason to keep its powder dry.

Summary:

  • China’s monthly loan prime rate fixing is due on Tuesday, with the one-year LPR expected to stay at 3.0% and the five-year at 3.5%.
  • A hold would make it the 17th straight month without a change; both tenors were last cut in May 2025.
  • The LPR is compiled from submissions by 20 designated banks; the one-year rate underpins most loans and the five-year rate guides mortgage pricing.
  • The LPRs take their cue from the PBOC’s seven-day reverse repo rate, its main policy rate since a mid-2024 framework change.
  • Monday’s data showed Q3 GDP growth of 4.5%, above forecasts, with retail sales and industrial output also beating expectations.
  • A Reuters poll sees the LPRs and the reserve requirement ratio unchanged through the first quarter of 2027.

China is expected to leave its benchmark lending rates unchanged at Tuesday’s monthly fixing, which would extend the hold to a 17th consecutive month, after stronger-than-expected third-quarter growth eased pressure on Beijing to add monetary support. The one-year loan prime rate is seen staying at 3.0% and the five-year LPR at 3.5%, with the fixing due at 9:00 a.m. Beijing time (0100 GMT / 2100 US Eastern time).

The loan prime rate is China’s benchmark for domestic lending and the reference point for pricing new bank loans. It is compiled each month from rate submissions by a panel of 20 designated commercial banks, although the People’s Bank of China retains strong influence over the outcome. There are two tenors: the one-year LPR, on which most new and outstanding loans are based, and the five-year LPR, which serves as the reference for mortgage pricing. The LPR replaced China’s old benchmark lending rate in August 2019 as part of a shift toward more market-based rate setting.

In practice, the LPR follows the central bank’s lead. Since a framework change in mid-2024, the PBOC has treated its seven-day reverse repo rate as its main policy rate, replacing the medium-term lending facility rate that previously served as the anchor for banks’ submissions. When the seven-day rate moves, the LPRs typically follow, and with it unchanged, the benchmarks have stayed put. Both tenors were last cut in May 2025, by 10 basis points each, following a larger quarter-point reduction in October 2024.

Monday’s data strengthened the case for patience. Gross domestic product grew 4.5% from a year earlier in the third quarter, slightly ahead of forecasts and up from 4.3% in the second quarter, lifting growth back to the bottom of Beijing’s 4.5% to 5% target range. September retail sales and industrial output also beat expectations, though property investment fell by around 21% in the first nine months of the year, underlining the weakness in housing. A Reuters poll conducted ahead of the release found economists expect the LPRs and the reserve requirement ratio to remain unchanged through the first quarter of 2027.

External conditions also argue against a cut. The Federal Reserve raised rates in September and signalled more could follow, widening the policy gap with China, and the premium on 10-year US Treasuries over Chinese government bonds was near a record high last month. Further easing would risk adding pressure on the yuan. At home, policymakers face weak credit demand and squeezed bank margins, which limit the appeal of lower lending rates.

A hold would keep attention on fourth-quarter data and on whether Beijing leans on liquidity measures or fiscal support rather than rate cuts if growth falters again.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump approval falls to record low. Poll shows Republicans losing badly in midterms
item.description:
Republicans are running out of time to turn it around ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

Trump is increasingly a liability of the party as his approval hits a record low of just 31%. It's an ugly chart as it continues to deteriorate with an inflection following the March war in Iran.

Worse yet is the broader polling trend:

  • Democrats lead Republicans 47% to 35% on the generic congressional ballot.

  • That 12-point advantage is the largest of the current election cycle, according to Reuters/Ipsos.

The generic ballot doesn’t translate directly into seats but that is an uncomfortable gap for Republicans. If it carries through to election day, it points to an acrimonious final two years for Trump in the White House, including investigations on Epstein, the Iran war and corruption.

For markets, it's likely that Democrat control of the House has been priced in for some time but a complete rout could kick off a broader repudation of Trump, even by his own party. That could strengthen the agenda for peace in the Middle East and an end to the trade war. At the same time, Trump under constant investigations could make him more impulsive and combative.

There is also the question of how Trump responds to deteriorating polling and how he wants to manage his legacy. Does it encourage a more conciliatory approach aimed at delivering economic wins, or a harder push on his least-popular policies? Will he want to be remembered as the President that started an endless war with Iran?

I would be careful about treating this as an immediate dollar or equity-market signal. The more useful takeaway is that the risk of a constrained White House is becoming harder to ignore and we count down to the vote.

The poll was taken over four days ending today.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDJPY buyers land the punches, but sellers are still standing
item.description:
Sellers have repeatedly defended the ceiling

The USDJPY technical story since September 23 has centered on two key levels: the 50% midpoint of the decline from the July 2026 high to the September low at 158.419, and the 200-day moving average, currently at 158.565.

The midpoint has remained fixed, while the 200-day moving average (higher green line) has edged higher from around 158.42. Together, they have created a resistance area where sellers have repeatedly leaned against the market and pushed the price lower.

There have been at least 10 tests of that area, with three separate breaks above both technical levels. The highest reached 159.019 during the move that began on September 24. Another reached 158.72 on October 12.

On each break, the buyers had their shot. Each time, they failed to sustain the momentum.

The downside rotations have varied, with swing lows near 157.524 and 157.425 helping to define the lower portion of the battle. Most of the price action has stayed inside the red box on the chart.

What the range teaches us

An important lesson in my book Attacking Currency Trends is to use technical tools to define risk and judge who has control.

When a recognizable midpoint and a longer-term moving average sit close together, they create a useful decision area. Sellers can lean against that area because it gives them a reference for where their trade starts to look wrong. Buyers know that getting above—and staying above—would strengthen their case.

The levels define the risk. The price action around them tells us whether that risk is being rewarded.

So far, the repeated failures above resistance tell us that buyers have struggled to turn a breakout into a trend. A move through a level is the first step. Follow-through, and the ability to hold above that level on a corrective move, provide stronger evidence that control is changing.

The hourly moving averages are the shorter-term barometer

Inside the range sit the 100- and 200-hour moving averages—the blue and green lines on the chart.

Admittedly, the price has moved above and below those averages, sometimes respecting them and sometimes passing through with little hesitation. That is what a market in a range can do. Buyers and sellers bob and weave, but neither side delivers the knockout punch.

That also provides an educational point: a moving-average break inside a range can shift the short-term bias without confirming a broader trend. Traders still need to pay attention to the next resistance or support level.

Currently, the price has moved above both hourly moving averages near 158.18, putting the shorter-term advantage with the buyers. However, the rally has so far stalled ahead of the 200-day moving average. Sellers still have a fighting chance.

What would put either fighter in control?

For buyers, the next job is to clear the 200-day moving average at 158.565 and hold above it. That would strengthen the bullish bias and bring the prior failed-break highs back into focus, including 158.72 and 159.019.

For sellers, holding below the 200-day moving average keeps their defense intact. A move back below the 50% midpoint at 158.419 would take some momentum away from the buyers and put the focus back on the hourly moving averages near 158.18.

A sustained break below those averages would shift the shorter-term advantage back toward sellers and reopen the door toward the lower swing areas.

For now, the buyers are landing the punches, and the sellers are closer to the ropes. But both sides have taken a beating during this extended range. The buyers are showing strength. They still need to get through resistance—and stay through it—to take firmer control of the fight.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: CIBC cuts gold forecasts but still sees $5,500 in 2028
item.description:
Gold bulls are getting a reminder that geopolitical turmoil doesn't always send bullion higher. Sometimes the inflation and interest-rate consequences overwhelm the safe-haven bid and sometimes the point of accumulating gold reserves is to use them when a shock -- like a war -- hits.

That's the challenge running through CIBC's latest precious metals outlook. The bank has sharply lowered its forecasts as higher energy prices, a stronger US dollar and a more hawkish Federal Reserve complicate the trade. But it still sees a substantial recovery over the next two years.

In its October report, CIBC cuts its 2027 average gold forecast to US$5,200 an ounce from $6,500. Its 2028 estimate falls to $5,500 from $6,000, while the fourth-quarter 2026 forecast drops to $4,500 from $6,500.

Those are sizeable revisions but still leave CIBC comfortably above the consensus estimates included in the report: $4,620 for 2027 and $4,451 for 2028.

“Despite this monetary policy headwind, we believe elevated geopolitical risk, fiscal concerns and continued diversification away from US Treasuries will underpin gold demand and support a recovery through 2027 and 2028," CIBC writes.

Gold is at $4147 more than 25% below its early-year peak near $5,600. Against that reference point, its 2028 average forecast implies a recovery of roughly 29%. The problem is getting there.

The report describes a market where the US-Iran conflict has supported demand for protection while simultaneously pushing oil prices and inflation expectations higher. That has strengthened the dollar and pushed the Fed toward tighter policy, undermining a non-yielding asset.

For traders, it's an awkward combination. More geopolitical risk can help gold, but another energy-price shock can also reinforce the very rate expectations holding it back.CIBC identifies a potential way out:

“In our view, gold could benefit if economic growth weakens or inflation moderates sufficiently to allow the Fed to pivot toward a more accommodative policy path than is currently reflected in market expectations or the FOMC’s projections.”

That puts the inflation and growth data squarely in focus. A sustained recovery would be easier with some relief from real yields and the dollar.

There is also a significant investment-demand assumption behind the bullish forecasts. CIBC projects gold ETF demand of 1,000 tonnes in each of 2027 and 2028, compared with just 35 tonnes in 2026. It also expects central-bank purchases to reach 1,000 tonnes annually in those two years.

Silver gets an even bigger near-term downgrade. CIBC cuts its 2027 forecast to $85 an ounce from $120, although that remains well above the report's $66 consensus estimate.

Copper goes the other way, with CIBC raising its forecast to $6.50 a pound for the fourth quarter and both 2027 and 2028.

“Demand growth is increasingly driven by grid modernization, electrification, renewable energy and digital infrastructure while new supply remains constrained by long development timelines, capital inflation and operating disruptions.”

The distinction is useful. Copper's upgraded outlook rests on physical demand and constrained supply. Gold's recovery depends more heavily on investment flows and how the monetary-policy backdrop evolves.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Broader tech focused indices are higher. How are some of the Magnificent 7 fairing technically?

item.title: Oil reverses course higher after US and Houthi attacks
item.description:
Oil prices have reversed higher in light of fresh reports about two separate Middle East strikes. WTI had traded down to $99.24 earlier and brent to $106.82, both after the US waived santions on Russian fuel.

That move now seems to have bought about 15 hours of lower oil prices and now crude is up on the day, with WTI at $103.13 and brent just above $110. 

Two stories have driven the gains, the first is that the Iranian navy said the US attacked the Konarek naval base with "two light projectiles" early this morning and that wo solidiers were injured. 

More recently, a pair of reports highlight that Houthis claimed six attacks on Saudi Arabia in the past 48 hours, including strikes on the Yanbu oil facility owned by Aramco, the Shaybah oilfield and airports in Ryiadh and Abha. Today, Saudi Arabia cancelled this year's 'Davos in the Desert' conference.

The next quesion is what will be the retaliation for the latest strikes on both sides. The US hadn't attacked Iran in seven weeks; Trump also said no attacks before the midterms. item.title: Bank of Canada Q3 business outlook survey -0.33 vs -0.38 prior
item.description:
• BOS indicator -0.33 vs -0.38 in Q2 (revised from -0.39)
  • Future sales balance of opinion +42 vs +15 in Q2
  • 18% of firms report an outright decline in sales over the past 12 months vs 22% in Q2
  • 6% of firms expect a recession in the next year vs 17% in Q2
  • 41% of firms expect inflation above 3% over the next two years vs 44% in Q2
  • Consumers’ 5-year inflation expectations 3.91% vs 3.39% in Q2
  • 53.0% of consumers expect a recession in the next 12 months vs 54.6% in Q2

Roughly three-quarters of the Business Outlook Survey interviews were done before Canada-US trade talks broke down and Ottawa announced new counter-tariffs so this data is already stale. The same goes for the consumer survey, where about three-quarters of responses came in before the August 21 breakdown. I'd argue that the 'breakdown' wasn't that damaging but that's up for debate.

In any case, the snapshot was decent. The jump in the future sales balance to +42 from +15 is a big move, and firms credited an easing of trade tensions and less Middle East risk.

Exporters were leaning on solid US demand and high oil prices. Investment intentions eased only slightly and remain robust. Hiring is the soft spot, with most firms planning to hold headcount flat.

The Bank of Canada addressed the timing problem head-on in a box looking at results collected after the talks collapsed. In the survey view, the new US tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs are weighing on outlooks for exports and investment, pushing up costs and prices, and inflation expectations have risen alongside the tariffs and the rebound in energy. The BOC wrote:

Firms surveyed after trade talks broke down reported weaker sentiment and lower expectations for export sales than those surveyed beforehand. These recent results suggest that some of the improvement in firms’ outlooks reported earlier in the third quarter of 2026 has reversed. Nevertheless, sentiment and expectations remain considerably stronger than at the height of trade tensions in 2025, suggesting a moderation rather than a fundamental shift in firms’ outlooks.

Firms’ input and selling price expectations moderated but remain elevated, mostly tied to oil and trade. More worrying for the BoC: companies facing big cost increases plan to keep passing them on, and some see improved demand as the window to claw back margins they gave up earlier. That’s the kind of behaviour that keeps inflation sticky.

Consumer survey 

The real red flag is on the consumer side. Five-year inflation expectations jumped more than half a point to 3.91%, rising to match elevated short-term expectations.

Long-run expectations catching up to short-run ones is exactly the de-anchoring central banks lose sleep over. And again, the BoC says expectations at all horizons moved higher after talks broke down, so the true number is likely worse.

Households reported better financial health thanks to asset gains and a bit more labour market confidence, but spending plans deteriorated from already-weak levels. High prices and uncertainty are the culprits. Interestingly, labour market perceptions improved for workers exposed to US trade but worsened for those in jobs at higher risk of AI task replacement.

Today's CPI data was a good sign for the Bank of Canada but this survey raises some hawkish questions.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Stock market shows an interesting hidden hint about investor confidence coming into earnings
item.description:
Earnings season heats up: Are investors beginning to reward good results again?

Wall Street's earnings season began cautiously, with investors punishing disappointments more severely than they rewarded positive surprises. But fresh trading activity on October 19 suggests that sentiment may be stabilizing. With Netflix, Tesla and Meta preparing to report, the next question is whether investors are becoming more willing to reward strong corporate results, or whether this improvement is only temporary.

Early earnings reactions were more negative than positive

The third-quarter earnings reporting season, taking place during the fourth quarter of 2026, began with some uncomfortable signals for stock market bulls.

An investingLive review of earnings reactions from October 13-16 identified several signs of a selective and defensive market:

  • Three of the four trading sessions produced negative capitalization-weighted earnings reactions, meaning larger companies had a greater influence on the results.

  • Downside moves exceeding options-implied expectations outnumbered upside surprises by 11 to 6.

  • Investors were not consistently rewarding corporate earnings announcements, even as individual companies continued reporting solid business performance.

These observations matter because good earnings are not necessarily enough to make a stock rise.

A company may report higher revenue, stronger profits and encouraging business developments, yet still see its shares decline.

Why?

Because stock prices reflect expectations about the future, not just the financial results being announced today. If investors were already expecting an exceptional quarter, a merely good quarter may disappoint.

The opposite can also happen. A company with relatively modest results may see its shares rally if investors feared something much worse.

October 19: The first encouraging signs?

The latest October 19 intraday earnings reactions offer a somewhat more constructive picture.

Among six companies with usable earnings reactions in the supplied investingLive analysis:

  • Four stocks advanced, while two declined.

  • Positive breadth reached 66.7%, meaning two-thirds of the companies gained.

  • The capitalization-weighted reaction was approximately +1.20%.

  • None of the five companies with comparable options-implied expected moves had exceeded its estimated range at the observation time.

This is an improvement worth watching, but not yet a decisive turnaround.

The most interesting distinction is that stocks were rising without necessarily producing unusually large upside surprises.

An options-implied move is an estimate of how far a stock might move around an event, inferred from options prices. When a stock moves beyond that range, the reaction may indicate that investors are repricing the company more dramatically than the options market had anticipated.

October 19's early data shows more stocks participating on the upside, but not yet evidence of exceptional positive repricing.

That difference matters.

It could be the beginning of stabilization. Alternatively, it could simply represent a relatively favorable collection of companies reporting on one particular day.

The October 19 observations are intraday snapshots, not final closing returns. The sample is also small and has not established a confirmed change in the broader earnings environment.

Cleveland-Cliffs and Fifth Third offer encouraging examples

Two companies illustrate how different types of corporate results can attract buyers.

Cleveland-Cliffs (CLF): A stronger outlook captures attention

The steel producer's shares were up approximately 7.84% in the supplied October 19 intraday snapshot.

Cleveland-Cliffs reported a substantial improvement in third-quarter profitability and presented a more optimistic earnings outlook. That combination gives investors something beyond the reported quarter to assess: whether the company's future profitability may improve more than previously expected.

The relevant question now is whether buyers maintain their enthusiasm beyond the immediate reaction.

A strong first-day gain is encouraging, but holding that gain over subsequent sessions would provide stronger evidence of sustained investor interest.

Fifth Third Bancorp (FITB): Banking resilience gets a measured response

Fifth Third gained approximately 1.42% in the supplied snapshot.

The regional banking group reported resilient credit performance, sequential growth in net interest income and progress integrating Comerica.

Its more measured share-price reaction illustrates another aspect of this earnings season: investors may be receptive to improving fundamentals without necessarily bidding shares sharply higher.

Elsewhere, the picture remains mixed. Recent rolling weekly performance has been comparatively strong for Ericsson, while Charles Schwab, Interactive Brokers and Prologis have experienced further weakness.

Those weekly returns are not isolated earnings reactions, but they reinforce the importance of evaluating individual companies rather than assuming that the entire market is moving together.

Netflix earnings on October 20: A test of expectations

Netflix (NFLX) reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, October 20.

Investors will be examining whether the streaming company can sustain growth while defending profitability and maintaining engagement in an increasingly competitive entertainment market.

The important questions include:

Engagement and revenue: Is Netflix generating sufficient revenue growth from its audience, advertising business and programming investments?

Profitability: Can the company maintain attractive margins while competing for viewers and spending on content?

Guidance: Does management's outlook support the growth expectations already embedded in the share price?

Even a headline earnings beat may not be enough if management's forward outlook disappoints.

For existing shareholders, the result may help assess whether the longer-term investment thesis remains intact. For traders, the initial share-price reaction and its ability to hold could be just as informative as the reported numbers themselves.

Tesla and Meta on October 21: Two different tests of investor confidence

Wednesday brings two major earnings announcements, each carrying broader market implications.

Tesla (TSLA): How much future growth is already priced in?

Tesla investors face several important questions, including automotive profitability, demand, energy storage growth and investment in future technologies.

The company's October 2 delivery report showed more than 486,000 vehicles delivered during the third quarter. However, vehicle deliveries alone do not establish profitability.

Investors will want to understand how sales volumes translate into margins, cash flow and management's outlook.

A strong reaction could indicate that investors are willing to look beyond near-term spending pressures. A disappointing reaction could suggest that the market is becoming less patient with ambitious future-growth expectations.

Meta Platforms (META): Is AI spending delivering sufficient returns?

Meta presents a different challenge.

Its advertising business provides an established source of profitability, while investment in artificial intelligence and supporting infrastructure creates additional spending demands.

The central question is whether advertising growth and business efficiency are sufficient to justify the scale of investment.

Positive operating results accompanied by higher spending projections could produce a complicated market response.

Strong profitability, credible guidance and evidence that investment is creating value would provide a more constructive combination.

Because these businesses influence major stock indices, their earnings reactions could also affect sentiment beyond their own shareholders.

What could confirm an improving earnings environment?

Rather than declaring earnings season bullish or bearish based on one favorable session, traders and investors can watch for three developments.

1. More stocks rising after earnings

If positive breadth persists across a larger and more diverse group of reporting companies, it would strengthen the case that investor sentiment is improving.

2. More meaningful upside reactions

Positive share-price moves are encouraging. But repeated moves exceeding options-implied expectations would suggest investors are becoming more willing to revalue companies upward.

3. Stocks holding their gains

One of the most useful tests comes after the initial excitement.

If a stock rallies following earnings and retains much of that advance over the following sessions, it suggests that buyers are continuing to support the new valuation.

Conversely, repeated reversals of initial rallies would indicate that enthusiasm remains fragile.

The same principle applies to negative reactions. A stock that initially falls but subsequently recovers can provide evidence that sellers are losing influence, although one recovery alone does not prove a durable bottom.

What if the improvement fails?

There is an important alternative scenario.

October 19's stronger reactions could prove temporary, especially if upcoming large-company reports disappoint investors.

Warning signs would include a renewed deterioration in earnings-reaction breadth, more stocks falling beyond their expected trading ranges, and strong companies struggling to hold gains after reporting.

The next wave of technology earnings will provide important evidence.

Microsoft and Alphabet are scheduled to report on October 28, followed by Amazon on October 29. Their cloud operations, AI-related investment and profitability outlooks will offer additional insight into how investors are assessing some of the market's most influential businesses.

The key takeaway for traders and investors

The most useful question this earnings season may not be simply, "Did the company beat expectations?"

It may be:

"Did investors reward the results, and did they continue to reward them after the initial reaction?"

For existing shareholders, earnings provide an opportunity to reassess business fundamentals, valuation and the longer-term investment case. A short-term price decline does not automatically invalidate an otherwise sound business thesis.

For traders and investors considering new positions, it can be useful to distinguish the immediate reaction from subsequent price behavior. A sharp move can create an opportunity, but it can also introduce significant risk when volatility and uncertainty are elevated.

As of October 19, the earnings environment remains selective, with tentative signs of stabilization rather than a confirmed bullish shift.

Netflix, Tesla and Meta may provide some of the clearest evidence yet of whether investors are becoming more willing to reward good corporate performance.

And for the broader stock market, that distinction could matter more than the number of companies that beat analysts' estimates.

item.title: US NAHB housing market index 29 vs 31 prior
item.description:
• Priorw as 32
  • Current sales 33 vs 35 prior
  • Sales over the next six months 32 vs 37 prior
  • Prospective buyers 18 vs 23 prior

The latest survey found that 43% of builders cut prices in October, the highest share during the 2020-2026 period. The average price cut remained at 6% for the seventh consecutive month. Meanwhile, 65% of builders reported using sales incentives in October, the 19th straight month at least 60% of builders have done so.

This is a response to yet-another rise in borrowing costs, with US mortages nearing 7.5% on a 30-year fixed in the period.

For background, The NAHB Housing Market Index is a monthly survey of homebuilder sentiment published by the National Association of Home Builders. It’s released around mid-month at 10 am ET, usually the day before the government’s housing starts report, which makes it the earliest read on the US housing market each month.

The index is built from a survey of NAHB members, focused on builders of single-family homes. They rate three conditions: current sales of new homes, expected sales over the next six months and traffic of prospective buyers. The responses are combined into a headline index running from 0 to 100. A reading of 50 is the dividing line, with anything above it meaning more builders view conditions as good than poor. The traffic component historically runs well below the other two and rarely tops 50 even in strong markets. NAHB also publishes regional readings for the Northeast, Midwest, South and West as three-month moving averages.

In recent years the survey’s added questions on price cuts and sales incentives have become some of its most useful details. They show how much builders are discounting or buying down mortgage rates to keep homes moving, information the headline doesn’t capture.

The index is highly sensitive to mortgage rates and affordability, and it tends to lead housing starts and building permits. It rarely moves broader markets on its own, but it’s watched closely by homebuilder stocks and as an early signal for residential investment, a key swing factor in GDP. Builders’ commentary on construction costs, including lumber, materials and tariffs, also feeds into the inflation picture.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDCAD bounces after softer CPI data but they have work to do.
item.description:
Canada’s September CPI report gave traders a little something on both sides of the inflation debate.

Headline inflation rose to 3.1% year over year from 3.0% in August, but came in below expectations of 3.2%. Meanwhile, inflation excluding gasoline slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%.

Energy remains the problem area. Gasoline prices increased 27.8% from a year earlier, while fuel oil and other fuels surged 57.8%, with a greater impact on households in Atlantic Canada. Shelter inflation also accelerated, although rent growth held steady and mortgage interest costs continued to decline.

The better news came from groceries. Annual inflation slowed to 1.7%, the lowest since May 2024, with fresh vegetables and sugar and confectionery prices declining from a year earlier. That is welcome relief, but slower inflation does not undo the earlier increases. Grocery prices remain 33.0% above September 2020 levels.

What does it mean for the Bank of Canada?

The headline moved higher, but energy drove the acceleration. The question for the Bank of Canada is whether those higher costs spread into other prices.

Slower inflation excluding gasoline offers some reassurance. However, the 0.4% seasonally adjusted monthly increase warrants attention.

For currency traders, higher inflation would normally support Canadian yields and the Canadian dollar, putting downward pressure on USDCAD. The softer-than-expected headline and slower non-gasoline inflation temper that argument.

So, what are the technicals telling traders?

Sellers have control. Can buyers defend 1.4082?

USDCAD moved lower ahead of the report, reaching a session low of 1.4071. That took the price below the 38.2% retracement at 1.40818 of the rally from the August 21 low to the October highs near 1.42984.

Following the report, the price recovered to 1.41119, but that bounce faded. The pair is back below 1.4100, trading near 1.4095.

For buyers, holding above 1.40818 is the first requirement. It gives them a level to lean against and define risk. It does not, by itself, put them in control.

A move back below that level—and staying below—would keep the sellers firmly in charge. The session low at 1.4071 would come back into focus, followed by the 100-day moving average at 1.40377. The price has not traded below that moving average since September 16.

Broken support becomes resistance

On the topside, buyers first need to get above the post-report corrective high near 1.4112.

Above that sits a more important swing area between 1.41297 and 1.41532. That zone has defined turning points going back to November 2025 and again between June 19 and July 14 this year.

The price broke above it on September 28. Now that USDCAD is back below, what was support becomes resistance.

Getting above that area—and staying above—would give buyers a stronger say in the direction.

Right now, however, they have work to do. Sellers remain in control, and 1.4082 is the short-term barometer. Stay above, and buyers can try to build a recovery. Move below, and the door opens for another shove lower.

In the video, I walk through the levels that define the risk, the bias, and the next targets for USDCAD.

For background, Statistics Canada publishes the Consumer Price Index monthly, usually in the third week of the following month at 8:30 am ET. It measures price changes for a fixed basket of goods and services bought by Canadian households, covering shelter, food, transportation, household operations, clothing, health, recreation and alcohol and tobacco.

Unlike in the US, the market’s focus is the year-over-year change in the unadjusted index rather than the seasonally adjusted monthly change, though both are published. The Bank of Canada targets 2% total CPI inflation, the midpoint of a 1% to 3% control range, and its mandate is framed around that headline measure.

Because headline inflation can be distorted by volatile items like gasoline and food, the Bank also watches its preferred core measures, CPI-trim and CPI-median. CPI-trim excludes the components with the most extreme price moves each month. CPI-median takes the price change at the 50th percentile of the basket. Markets often look at the average of the two. Other core gauges include CPIX and CPI excluding food and energy.

Shelter is the largest component and a frequent source of noise. It includes mortgage interest cost, which creates a quirk in the data: when the Bank raises interest rates, mortgage costs rise and push measured inflation higher, at least temporarily. Rent and homeowners’ replacement cost are also closely watched.

Canadian CPI is one of the most market-moving domestic releases, with surprises in the core measures in particular able to shift Bank of Canada rate pricing and move the Canadian dollar. With the US the dominant trading partner, tariffs and exchange-rate swings have become an important channel for imported inflation

item.title: Why do central banks target 2% inflation instead of 0%?
item.description:
Most major central banks have a clearly defined inflation target around 2% per year over the medium term. But why they don't aim for 0%, so that prices remain unchanged over time?  The answer lies in how inflation expectations influence economic decisions, the risks associated with deflation and the limitations of monetary policy.

An inflation target provides a clear reference point for households, businesses and financial markets. This matters because expectations influence behaviour. Businesses consider expected inflation when setting prices and negotiating wages. Workers take expected changes in the cost of living into account when negotiating salaries. Households factor expected inflation into decisions about consumption, saving and borrowing, while investors incorporate it into bond yields and other asset prices.

When the public trusts that a central bank will keep inflation close to its target, expectations are more likely to remain anchored around that level. This helps prevent temporary price shocks from turning into persistent inflation.

Take the increase in oil prices as an example. Higher energy costs can push headline inflation up temporarily. If households and businesses believe the central bank will bring inflation back towards 2%, they may be less inclined to demand permanently higher wages or raise prices aggressively in anticipation of further inflation. This makes the initial shock less likely to spread throughout the economy.

The opposite can happen when confidence in the inflation target deteriorates. If workers expect prices to keep rising, they may demand larger wage increases. Businesses facing higher labour costs may then raise their prices, reinforcing inflationary pressures. Central banks may have to raise interest rates more aggressively to break this cycle.

An inflation target acts as an anchor for expectations. It does not eliminate economic shocks, but it can help prevent those shocks from becoming self-reinforcing.

Why target 2% instead of 0%?

There are several reasons why a modestly positive inflation rate is preferable. The first is to create a buffer against deflation. Deflation occurs when the general price level falls persistently. Although falling prices might initially seem beneficial to consumers, widespread and sustained deflation can create serious economic problems.

When people expect prices to fall further, they may postpone purchases. Businesses can respond to weaker demand by reducing investment, cutting production and laying off workers. Lower incomes can then weaken demand further, putting additional downward pressure on prices and the economy.

Deflation also increases the real burden of debt. A household or business that borrowed money must still repay the same nominal amount, even if the prices of the goods and services it sells are falling. Revenues and wages may decline while debt repayments remain unchanged, making existing loans more difficult to service.

This can create a damaging feedback loop between falling prices, weaker demand, declining incomes and financial stress. A 2% inflation target provides a margin of safety. Inflation fluctuates around its target as the economy experiences changes in demand, supply disruptions and other shocks. If the target were 0%, a relatively small negative shock could push the economy into deflation immediately. With a positive target, central banks have more room to absorb these fluctuations without falling into deflation.

Inflation and real interest rates

Another reason central banks target positive inflation is that it helps preserve room to stimulate the economy by lowering real interest rates. What matters for economic activity is not just the nominal interest rate set by a central bank, but also how that rate compares with inflation. Real interest rates measure the cost of borrowing after accounting for the erosion of purchasing power caused by inflation. The real interest rate is approximately the nominal interest rate minus expected inflation.

When inflation exceeds the nominal interest rate, real interest rates are negative. This makes borrowing relatively cheap in real terms and reduces the real burden of existing nominal debt, supporting consumption, investment and credit growth. Conversely, when nominal interest rates exceed inflation, real rates are positive, making borrowing more expensive in real terms and encouraging saving over spending. This tends to restrain demand and slow economic activity.

Central banks therefore influence the economy partly by adjusting nominal rates relative to inflation expectations. When growth weakens, they can cut nominal rates to reduce real borrowing costs and provide stimulus. However, their ability to do so becomes more constrained when nominal rates are already close to zero.

This is where a positive inflation target becomes important. If inflation expectations are anchored around 2%, nominal interest rates can generally settle at a higher level over time than they would in an economy with a 0% inflation target, all else being equal. This gives central banks more room to cut nominal rates during a downturn, lowering real rates and making monetary conditions more accommodative.

A zero inflation target would leave less of a buffer against deflation. If inflation expectations fell below zero while nominal rates were already near zero, real interest rates could rise even without any increase in nominal rates. Monetary conditions would become more restrictive precisely when the economy might need additional support. This is what happened during the Great Depression as deflation drove real interest rates higher and made the economic downturn much worse.

A positive inflation target helps reduce this risk. It does not guarantee that real rates will always be low enough to stimulate growth, but it provides a buffer against deflation and gives central banks more flexibility to lower real borrowing costs when economic conditions deteriorate.

item.title: A breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations is expected to be announced this week, according to Al-Arabiya
item.description:
Al-Arabiya is saying that a breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations is expected to be announced this week as negotiators are working to narrow differences and secure mutual concessions to prevent a renewed escalation.

The timing of the report is interesting as we approach the US midterm elections due on November 3. Trump has a strong political incentive to end this costly conflict and ease pressure on energy prices, which have become a key source of concern for the American people. A breakthrough would send oil prices sharply lower on expected supply improvement and Strait of Hormuz reopening.

However, although the timing of the report could give markets hope for an imminent breakthrough, one should take it with a pinch of salt. Recent reporting hasn't been exactly rosy, with the US floating the idea of using the MOAB bomb.

Over the weekend, Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi reiterated that Tehran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days remains on the table. The proposal is conditional on US acceptance of Iran's demands, including lifting the blockade on Iranian ports, easing sanctions on Iranian oil exports and ending hostilities across the region. The two sides reportedly remain divided over the conditions and the order in which concessions should be implemented.

The central disagreement is whether the reopening of the strait and relief from US pressure should come before substantive concessions on Iran's nuclear programme. The US has insisted that Iran's nuclear activities must be addressed, while Tehran wants the immediate focus to be on maritime security and the removal of restrictions affecting its economy.

Trump has waived several Russian sanctions over the weekend in an attempt to lower energy prices, but the oil market has been driven primarily by the Middle East crisis. With WTI crude approaching the $100 level again and the widespread dissatisfaction, he could pull off a short-term deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and lift the US blockade ahead of the elections.

item.title: Connecting the dots: What falling luxury sales could be telling us about the US economy
item.description:
When most people look at designer bags, what do you think is the first thought that comes to mind? I'd wager it would be along the lines of "nice, but absolutely not at that price". And that very moment of hesitation could actually tell us more about the economy than you might think.

Now, a luxury bag isn't like groceries or petrol. It is a want, not a need. But when people start thinking twice about those purchases, it is worth thinking about the bigger picture and whether consumer confidence is taking a hit.

According to Citi's credit card data released earlier this month, luxury spending fell 6% year-on-year in September. And that follows from the declines of 4% in both July and August before that. The data shows three consecutive months of weakness. So, that is not exactly encouraging especially when wealthy US consumers have been one of the more resilient groups in this economy.

Having said that, let's take a look at this. US retail sales actually rose by 0.8% in September, albeit largely bolstered by higher gasoline prices. But in excluding gasoline stations, retail sales still grew by 0.2%.

It's not extravagant but it still suggests that US consumers are still spending. However, that doesn't necessarily mean they are buying more stuff. It just means that their spending habits have perhaps changed.

So, how does this tie back to Wall Street?

Just imagine that you are running a luxury retailer. You've got expensive stores, employees and marketing bills to pay. And those costs don't disappear just because fewer customers are buying handbags. As such, slower sales mean less revenue to cover those expenses. And if you turn to promotions to attract customers, then your profit margins could get squeezed further.

Now, I'm not suggesting fewer handbag purchases mean a recession is coming. Luxury spending is only one piece of the consumer puzzle, and the wealthiest shoppers tend to behave differently from everyone else.

But if that hesitation starts spreading to the likes of clothing, electronics, travel and other discretionary purchases, then corporate earnings forecasts could be next in line for a reality check. And when investors start questioning how much consumers are really willing to spend, stock valuations can suddenly look rather expensive.

With that in mind, it's worth noting that sometimes the first economic warning can simply just be what is sitting unsold on a store shelf. And it could very well be the designer bag that the crowd chooses to pass on.
